video_title: Hedgeye Investing Summit Fall 2026 | David McAlvany, CEO & PM of McAlvany Financials Group
gist: At Hedgeye's Fall 2026 summit, David McAlvany argues the debt-financed AI buildout is a bubble likely to burst (citing Oracle's force majeure on a $165B Blue Owl project), and says sovereign-debt debasement plus central bank and trade-settlement demand set gold up for a major move, targeting $8,000 gold and about $200 silver within 2-3 years. Keith McCullough agrees on the secular case but times entry with his quad and dollar/rates signals, expecting a 3-6 month window after inflation peaks, much like the 2008 dollar-bounce pullback.

themes.theme: AI capex as a debt-financed bubble

insights.claim: McAlvany argues the AI buildout is the largest infrastructure project in US history, dwarfing canals, railroads, electrification, highways and the 1996-2003 telecom buildout, and that its bursting is close to inevitable based on the math.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Frames AI capex as the 'mother of all bubbles', with gold as a beneficiary once it bursts.
insights.quote: I think gold ends up playing a significant part on the other side of the AI bubble bursting

insights.claim: The AI bull case requires OpenAI and Anthropic to grow revenue roughly 80% annualized through 2032-2033 and the buildout to arrive on time and on budget; McAlvany sees that as unrealistic.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: The bull case rests on assumptions nobody can check; watch whether revenue growth keeps pace with capex.

insights.claim: Shifting AI infrastructure funding from equity to debt is the key risk: debt brings fixed interest costs that must be serviced before project revenue shows up, which creates a cash-flow mismatch.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Debt-funded capex makes the AI trade fragile to delays and to the cost of capital.
insights.quote: equity capital can be patient, but debt has to be paid

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are now issuing debt in five currencies, and AI-linked debt is landing in pension funds and insurers worldwide, which McAlvany likens to how MBS/ABS spread US mortgage risk globally in 2006-2007.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: An AI bust could spread through global credit markets, not just equities.
insights.quote: with your big hyperscalers issuing debt in five different [clears throat] currencies now.

insights.claim: McAlvany says the data centers planned through 2032 need a conservative 288 GW of power, roughly 143 new nuclear plants or about 30,000 wind turbines covering about 22.6 million acres, which he calls logistically unrealistic.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Power is the binding physical constraint on the AI buildout timeline.
insights.quote: conservative estimates 288 gawatts of power

insights.claim: About $3.7 trillion of revenue must be generated through 2032 to support AI equity and debt spending; a Wall Street Journal headline asked whether America will spend 9% of GDP on AI, which McAlvany notes is more than the US spends on food.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Gives a hurdle figure for testing whether AI revenue is on track.
insights.quote: you got to generate $3.7 trillion [clears throat] in revenue to support it.

insights.claim: The IIF counts about $500 billion of borrowed money for AI-linked companies, and JPMorgan projects another $4 trillion of borrowing for the buildout over the next five years.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: AI leverage is set to grow fast, which raises sensitivity to rates.

insights.claim: Chip packaging is a supply-chain bottleneck: even chips made in the US must be shipped to Asia for encapsulation before they can be racked, which adds timing risk.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Delays raise the chance of debt service coming due before revenue.

insights.claim: McAlvany points to an early crack: Oracle invoked force majeure on a $165 billion New Mexico data center project with Blue Owl, built on borrowed money against the Oracle lease, after the state would not grant a natural gas pipeline connection, though delivery was still 12-18 months away.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Oracle and its private credit partners are the first visible signs of stress.
insights.quote: forced majour with Oracle on the project just south of us in New Mexico, $165 billion project with Blue Owl.

insights.claim: McCullough says Oracle is one of Hedgeye's longest-standing bearish trend signals and a short on its list, which he calls unprecedented during a bull market in software; he tracks Oracle CDS, uranium and copper prices as real-time AI-bubble gauges.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Oracle stock and CDS serve as a leading public-market tell for the AI trade.
insights.quote: Oracle has been one of the longest standing bearish trend signals at hedgei it's a short

insights.claim: McCullough argues that uranium and nuclear stocks being 'nuked' while copper barely holds a bullish trend contradicts the narrative of huge AI power and materials demand.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Commodity prices are not confirming the AI demand story.
insights.quote: things like uranium and nuclear have been nuked

insights.claim: McAlvany compares today's AI vendor dynamics to Nortel, whose vendor financing flattered its numbers before collapsing, and recalls a 120-year-old family-connected fiber cable supplier that went bankrupt after WorldCom when Bank of America marked its inventory collateral at a discount.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Overcapacity becomes visible only in hindsight, and collateral values collapse with demand.
insights.quote: We don't know what overcapacity is until it's in the rearview mirror.

themes.theme: Equity concentration, foreign capital and the 2022 replay

insights.claim: McAlvany says market breadth is among the worst in 100 years and US margin debt is about $1.4-1.5 trillion, so a few AI winners are masking many S&P 500 stocks heading toward bear market territory.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Index highs hide fragility, and leverage makes a reversal sharper.
insights.quote: margin debt of over 1.4 almost 1.5 trillion dollars

insights.claim: Roughly a third of US stock market capitalization, about $20 trillion, is foreign capital, and McAlvany warns that even a small withdrawal could rupture equities.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Foreign flows are a key swing factor if US returns weaken.
insights.quote: roughly a third of current US stock market capitalization is foreign capital.

insights.claim: McAlvany expects a 2022-style replay in which stocks and bonds fall together, which undermines the classic de-risking move into bonds and supports Mike Wilson's 60/20/20 idea, with gold as the non-correlated asset.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Consider a gold sleeve in place of part of the bond allocation for stress periods.
insights.quote: I think a replay of 2022 is more likely where you've got pressure in both stocks and bonds

themes.theme: Gold timing: dollar, rates and the 2008 analog

insights.claim: McCullough notes gold is strongly inverse-correlated with the dollar on trending (90+ day) correlations, and that gold's all-time high near $5,419 coincided with a multi-year low in the dollar index; the dollar has since turned bullish on his trade and trend signals.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: A dollar bounce is the main near-term headwind for gold.

insights.claim: McAlvany sees chart support for gold around $4,000, where central banks have bought; a break below $3,900 opens downside to about $3,300, possibly alongside a strong dollar rally driven by a weak euro and yen.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Defines levels: $4,000 support, $3,900 trigger, $3,300 downside target.
insights.quote: I'd hate to see it get below 3900. You know, the charts open up to 3,300.

insights.claim: McCullough's 2008 analog: gold peaked at $911 as the dollar fell, corrected to about $710 when the dollar index bounced from 71 to 88, then rallied toward $1,900 by 2011 as the dollar resumed its downtrend; he expects the same 'whipsaw' pattern now.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Treats the current gold correction as a buying setup within a secular uptrend.

insights.claim: McCullough's roadmap for going big on physical gold: inflation peaks within about three months and is cut in half by Q2 of next year, which should break the dollar and rates; in 2007-2012 the 10-year yield fell from 5.3% to 1.4% as gold made new highs. He sees a 3-6 month window to buy.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete timing signal for adding gold aggressively.
insights.quote: inflation puts in its cycle peak sometime now in the next three months.

insights.claim: McCullough argues a bubble market is an alternative to gold, since investors chase what is rising, so gold tends to do best after a bubble pops, as after 1999 when gold bottomed in 2001-2002 and rose until 2011.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Positioning for gold should anticipate the end of the AI trade.
insights.quote: A bubble market is an alternative to buying gold, right?

insights.claim: McAlvany recalls that in late 2008 physical gold decoupled from paper: delivery premiums ran about 30% and dealers limited buyers to one kilo bar per client per day, so investors effectively did not get the paper-price drop.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: In a crisis, physical scarcity can override futures price declines.
insights.quote: it did in the paper contract market, but it didn't in the physical market

themes.theme: Structural gold demand: central banks and settlement

insights.claim: Since 2022, central bank gold buying has doubled from about 500 to about 1,000 tons a year, roughly 25% of annual mine supply, driven by a wish to protect their independence from the US Treasury and State Department.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Price-insensitive official demand reduces gold's reliance on the dollar correlation.

insights.claim: World Gold Council surveys show 45% of central banks are inclined to add gold this year, and 94% say they will cut their dollar positions over the next 12-24 months.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Points to sustained reserve diversification away from Treasuries.

insights.claim: McAlvany expects China's push to settle trade in local currencies, with gold as the net settlement mechanism (Jeff Currie's idea), to define gold over the next 3-5 years; the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is discussing doubling or tripling its vaulting capacity.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Gold's monetary role could expand beyond reserves into trade settlement.

insights.claim: McAlvany says 2025's gold rally was driven by central banks, not retail: McAlvany's business was average and retail queues appeared only in the last two weeks of December and first two of January, so premiums are low and product is the cheapest in 50 years despite high spot prices.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Retail demand has not arrived yet, which leaves room for a demand surge.
insights.quote: the elephant tracks have been central banks, not investors.

insights.claim: McAlvany argues debasement is 'mechanical and perpetual' (citing Jim Grant): with about $40 trillion of US debt, running 3-4% inflation against a 2% target is the only practical path, since 3% real growth is not enough.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Persistent inflation above target supports holding real assets for the long term.
insights.quote: There is no other way to address $40 trillion in debt.

insights.claim: US interest expense is about $1 trillion, roughly 25% of tax revenue; the average cost of debt is 3.44%, below the whole yield curve, so rollovers through 2028 will push interest costs higher, and $2 trillion of interest would be about 45% of tax revenue.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Rising interest costs push fiscal stress forward.
insights.quote: 3.44% is is the average interest expense across all durations which is well below the entire yield curve.

insights.claim: McAlvany says the Summers-Barsky thesis, that positive real yields pull money out of gold, assumes a functioning debt market; if sovereign credit quality comes into question, investors may prefer corporate over government debt, and the thesis can be 'put on hold'.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: High real yields may not cap gold if sovereign credit risk is being repriced.
insights.quote: you can take the Summers Barski thesis and put it on hold

insights.claim: Global government and other debt totals about $365 trillion, which McAlvany calls the true 'mother of all bubbles', and he notes 13 OECD members have debt-to-GDP as bad as or worse than the US (France about 119% versus US about 120%).
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Debasement is a global trend, not just a US one.

insights.claim: Asked about marking US gold reserves (over 8,100 tonnes, carried at $42/oz) to market, McAlvany says it would be a one-time balance sheet boost that leaves the income statement unchanged and would likely trigger an 'oh crap' moment in markets.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: A gold revaluation would signal fiscal stress, not fix it.
insights.quote: One time improvement to balance sheet is great, but your income statement still sucks.

themes.theme: Portfolio construction: gold, silver, miners, Bitcoin

insights.claim: McAlvany's allocation rule: decide what share of the portfolio to hold in liquidity, then split it half gold and half short-term T-bills, so part of your liquidity carries an inflation hedge.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: A simple, actionable sizing rule for gold.
insights.quote: I let every investor figure out what they want in liquidity and then divide by two.

insights.claim: McAlvany targets $8,000 gold over the next 2-3 years, implying about $200 silver; $10,000 gold implies about $250 silver and $12,000 gold about $350-400 silver, because the gold-silver ratio compresses at extremes.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Explicit price targets, with silver as the higher-beta way to play gold.
insights.quote: $8,000 gold over the next two, three years is is a reasonable price target.

insights.claim: Younger investors treat silver as 'gold with torque' and prefer miners, which can outperform the metal by 2-2.5x in the right conditions; McAlvany expects miners to 'blow people's minds', while central banks and family offices stick to more liquid gold.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Miners and silver offer leverage to the gold cycle, at the cost of more downside.
insights.quote: they look at silver as gold with torque

insights.claim: McAlvany sees room for a low single-digit Bitcoin allocation alongside gold within the debasement trade; Bitcoin's main risk is quantum computing threatening blockchain integrity, and it is untested in a global financial crisis.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Keep a small Bitcoin sleeve with sizing capped by its unproven crisis behavior.
insights.quote: the only challenge that Bitcoin has ahead of it is is navigating quantum computation

insights.claim: In a Mises-style crack-up boom, McAlvany says the Dow could reach twice its current level, gold five times and Bitcoin perhaps ten times, even as purchasing power erodes.
insights.speaker: David McAlvany
insights.so_what: Equities can rise in nominal terms during heavy debasement.

insights.claim: Under Hedgeye's quad framework, gold is best in Quad 1, decent in Quad 3, mediocre in Quad 4 and weakest in Quad 2, where Bitcoin and growth stocks thrive, which McCullough says explains why gold can fall while Bitcoin and growth stocks break out.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Match gold exposure to the macro quad; Quad 2 favors other assets.
insights.quote: Bitcoin loves quad 2. Gold does not like quad 2.

insights.claim: McCullough says he is currently short palladium and silver, will not short gold, and is waiting to buy gold, after earlier holding up to 9 of his 30 asset allocations in metals.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Shows a tactically bearish stance on metals now while he waits to buy gold.
insights.quote: now I'm short palladium and I'm short silver and I won't short gold
